q: How does one dollar provide a year of clean water, and what will the money raised actually achieve?
a: The one dollar for one year figure is a planning average. Clean water can cost anywhere from about $10 to $150 per person depending on the community and system needed, so WaterAid and partners designed a mix of projects averaging roughly $20 per person. The more than $40 million raised will reach around 2 million people, each with water systems built to last at least two decades, which is what the campaign means by tens of millions of years of clean water.

q: Which countries are the #TeamWater projects taking place in, and how were they chosen?
a: The work reaches communities in more than 20 countries across 5 continents, including Kenya, Tanzania, Brazil, Cambodia, Rwanda, the USA, Nigeria, Bangladesh, and Mozambique. WaterAid and partners choose each location and solution based on where the need is greatest and what will work best for that community.

q: What types of water systems are used, and why do they differ from one community to the next?
a: Solutions range from piped connections and solar-powered pumps to gravity-fed pipelines, rainwater harvesting, desalination or household filters. WaterAid and partners match the approach to each community's geography, climate, and needs, so the systems differ from place to place.

q: When did the projects begin, and when will communities start receiving clean water?
a: Work began in 2025 and will run for about 5 years. Some communities are already connected, while others are still in design, since WaterAid and partners often spend up to a year preparing with a community before building begins, so that the systems are built to last. Clean water arrives on a rolling basis, depending on the size and complexity of each project.

q: How will these water systems be maintained over time?
a: Long-term maintenance is planned into every project from the start. Water systems last when local people own and manage them and when funds, spare parts, and trained technicians are available for repairs. WaterAid and partners build around these factors, working with local communities and governments and training local technicians to keep systems running for years.

q: Who receives and manages the donated funds?
a: Donations are received and managed by WaterAid, the campaign's global partner, which implements programs directly in some countries and partners with local organizations in others, including GivePower in Kenya, the Alok Institute in Brazil, and DigDeep in the United States.
